items.title: Do People Trust AI Assistants Even When They Are Consistently Wrong?
items.evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
items.abstract_text: People are increasingly using conversational AI systems to make decisions despite concerns around their reliability. How well do people calibrate to AI systems' accuracy in multi-turn conversations? We measure how people's reliance on LLMs' advice changes across repeated interactions, varying whether the AI assistant is helpful (100% accurate), unhelpful (0% accurate), or mixed (50% accurate). Across 4 experiments, we find people learn to trust helpful models more than unhelpful ones (67% vs 21% of the time), but only when they receive external feedback on the models' accuracy. Without feedback, people continue to be persuaded 48% of the time by a consistently unhelpful model (vs 38% for helpful). Rather than gaining trust in helpful models, participant reliance on LLM advisors tended to be high in early trials and only fell with evidence of inaccuracy. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than they trusted human advisors (83% vs 65%, Experiment 4), and LLMs benefited more from having a helpful track record than humans did. In contrast with previous work, we find limited evidence of an advantage for arguing for the truth (versus a falsehood). Truth advantages emerged only when participants were already very confident in their position, and did not emerge at all for static hints. Collectively, the results suggest that people may be swayed by LLM advice, even when it is consistently false, unless they have access to timely ground-truth feedback. Unfortunately, in many domains such feedback may not be available, leading to overreliance on AI.

summary.idea: People used an AI adviser’s track record when they could check its answers.
summary.explain: Without a way to verify earlier answers, an apparently helpful conversation could still lead someone away from an initially correct judgment.
summary.approach: In a series of experiments, advisers discussed factual questions with participants. One experiment varied feedback about previous answers and whether people conversed or read hints.
summary.finding: In the conversation conditions of Experiment 3, earlier accuracy made a difference when feedback was available. Without feedback, even a previously inaccurate assistant persuaded people on 48% of the final trials.
summary.interpretation: An adviser’s fluency gives users little direct information about whether its past recommendations were correct.
summary.limitation: These were short factual tasks. The final challenge targeted an answer the participant had initially gotten right. The results do not measure lasting trust or behavior in other domains.

items.abstract_text: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

items.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
items.evidence: Preprint; source-checked v1, peer review unverified
items.abstract_text: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

items.title: Human tutoring, generative AI tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge
items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered. Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses. Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour. What this paper adds This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge. Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search. By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty. Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions. Implications for practice and/or policy Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help. The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty. The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty. Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in a large sixth-form college in England with a well-established digital infrastructure, including a bring-your-own-device policy, a dedicated digital leadership team and prior experience with custom-built educational GenAI tutors. Participants were aged 16-18. A total of 160 students volunteered and took part, representing approximately 5% of the college's population of around 3000. Recruitment was college-wide. The Director of Digital Strategy circulated invitations by email at several points during the academic year and a two-minute video in which the researcher explained the study and invited participation was shown during morning tutor time. Recruitment did not occur through particular subject lessons, although participation was self-selecting. Eleven participants were excluded because technical disruptions resulted in incomplete sessions or unusable data, yielding a quantitative analytic sample of 149. Usable post-task questionnaire responses were available for 154 participants (Human, n = 52; GenAI tutor, n = 52; Internet, n = 50) and were retained in a separate questionnaire dataset. Current A-level subject data were available for 144 of the 149 participants in the quantitative analytic sample. The most commonly studied subjects were Mathematics (n = 94, 65.3%), Psychology (n = 69, 47.9%), Biology (n = 43, 29.9%), Chemistry (n = 38, 26.4%), Physics (n = 37, 25.7%), Further Mathematics (n = 34, 23.6%) and Computer Science (n = 28, 19.4%). Participants could report multiple subjects. To assess baseline comparability following random allocation, participant characteristics were compared across the three conditions. Kruskal-Wallis tests identified no statistically significant differences in perceived socioeconomic status, GCSE mathematics grade, perceived mathematics ability or perceived mathematics ability relative to others (all ps ≥ 0.917). Chi-square tests likewise identified no significant associations between condition and baseline trait challenge-seeking category (p = 0.446), gender among female and male participants (p = 0.307), Mathematics participation (p = 0.606) or Further Mathematics participation (p = 0.871). The study used a single-site, three-condition, randomised between-subjects experimental design. Each participant had only one form of support and remained in that condition throughout. Random allocation was used to reduce the likelihood of systematic baseline differences between the condition groups and thereby strengthen the internal validity of the comparison (Clark et al., 2026) . Participants were individually allocated using a randomnumber generator to one-to-one human tutor, GenAI tutor or independent internet search. The quantitative analytic sample comprised 52 participants in the Human condition, 50 in the GenAI tutor condition and 47 in the Internet condition. All participants were presented with the same fixed sequence within a 90-min session: two 20-min sections of increasingly challenging mathematics problems ( S1 and S2 ), inspired by the PERC task (Porter et al., 2020) , followed by a behavioural challenge-selection task adapted from Rege et al. (2021) . Materials, task order, timings and outcome measures were held constant across conditions. Participants were instructed to use the support for guidance and not to seek direct answers. Participants in the GenAI tutor condition additionally received verbal and written guidance on using the tutor, including instructions not to enter personal data. The two-section structure was designed to examine how students responded when required to return to a new round of challenge after an earlier encounter with substantial difficulty. Effort, perceived difficulty and the number of questions attempted were recorded for each section. Task-related stress was assessed after the problem-solving sections, and behavioural challenge-seeking was assessed through the subsequent selection task. Students attended a single 90-min session conducted in a small teaching room within the college and completed the study individually on their own devices using a standardised Qualtrics platform. After instructions emphasising that tasks were intentionally challenging and optional, participants completed S1 with their assigned support, followed by effort and difficulty ratings, then S2 and the same measures. They then completed the challengeseeking task and a post-task questionnaire. The researcher was present to ensure procedural consistency. As an incentive for participation, all students were entered into a prize draw to win one of five £20 gift vouchers.
analysis.results: Findings are reported first for condition differences in perceived difficulty, effort, attempts and challenge-seeking, followed by task-related stress and changes across the two task sections. Tables 1 and 2 present the descriptive and inferential results, with significant omnibus differences examined using Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons.
analysis.discussion: The capacity of generative AI to independently complete many traditional academic tasks calls into question the educational value of using such tasks as primary indicators of learning (Corbin, Dawson, et al., 2025; Corbin, Walton, et al., 2025) . In response, there is growing consensus that evaluations of AI in education should move beyond grades to attend more closely to how learning is enacted and to the development of higher-order human capacities in human-AI interaction (Luckin, 2018 (Luckin, , 2025;; OECD, 2019 OECD, , 2025;; Wegerif & Major, 2024) . By foregrounding learners' effort, perceived difficulty, behavioural engagement and affective responses, the present study responds directly to these concerns by examining how learning is experienced and regulated under different support conditions. Even with identical tasks, the Human, GenAI tutor and Internet groups differed in their patterns of perceived difficulty, effort and attempts, while stress-response distributions varied descriptively. Consistent with long-standing critiques of performance-based assessment (Bjork & Bjork, 2011 , 2020; Marton & Saljo, 1976; Wegerif & Major, 2024) , the present findings further underscore the value of examining how students travel through learning, not just where they end up. As calls grow to prioritise the development of wider human capacities essential for learning (Luckin, 2025) , understanding these behavioural trajectories becomes critical. The findings did not support the preregistered directional hypothesis overall, as support from the GenAI tutor used in this study did not produce consistently higher effort, a greater number of attempted questions or greater challenge-seeking than the comparison conditions. Given the differences between the preregistered and implemented study, the precise outcome-and section-specific findings are interpreted as exploratory. The variation in effort, perceived difficulty and attempts across conditions suggests that some aspects of students' responses while working through challenge may be shaped by the form of interactive support available during learning, consistent with prior work on the role of framing and interaction in shaping engagement with difficulty (Duckworth, 2016; Duckworth et al., 2007; Dweck, 2006; Hadwin et al., 2018; Young et al., 2024 ). Crucially, these findings extend prior accounts by showing that these response patterns may also differ when support is provided by a GenAI tutor. Students working with the GenAI tutor used in this study reported the highest and most stable effort across sections, although the between-condition difference was significant only in Section 2, when effort was higher than in the Human condition. This higher effort co-occurred with greater perceived difficulty than under human tutoring. One possible interpretation is that the GenAI tutor used in this study helped students continue investing effort despite finding the tasks difficult, suggesting that this form of GenAI support may help sustain engagement during challenging independent work. However, higher effort could also reflect the additional exertion required when difficulty remained unresolved. Self-reported effort is not inherently positive or negative. Higher effort may indicate willingness to persist, but it may also reflect unresolved difficulty or a greater need for exertion. Conversely, lower effort may indicate disengagement, but it may also mean that less exertion was required because support made the task more manageable. The findings therefore cannot determine whether this effort represented productive persistence or difficulty that the support had not adequately alleviated. Effort was therefore interpreted alongside perceived difficulty and attempts, rather than as a standalone indicator of the quality or success of students' engagement. In the separate post-task questionnaire, the GenAI tutor condition descriptively contained a lower proportion of stressed responses than the Internet condition. As no inferential comparisons were conducted, this pattern cannot establish that GenAI tutor support reduced stress, but it is consistent with prior work suggesting that AI-supported struggle may reduce frustration, support motivation and help regulate cognitive load (Bassner et al., 2026) . The GenAI tutor condition also showed the largest descriptive increase in attempts from the first to the second section. Although co-regulation was not measured directly, the combined pattern of reported effort, perceived difficulty, attempts and stress responses is consistent with the possibility that interaction with the GenAI tutor contributed to students' regulation of behavioural engagement and affect as they worked through unresolved difficulty. This interpretation aligns with conceptual accounts that position generative AI as a potential participant in distributed co-regulatory systems (Lodge et al., 2023; Nguyen, 2025) . Consistent with expectations from scaffolding and co-regulation theory (Gaffney & Rodgers, 2018; Hadwin et al., 2018; Vygotsky, 1978; Wood et al., 1976; Wood & Wood, 1996) , the Human condition produced the most favourable difficulty profile, with students reporting the lowest perceived difficulty in both sections. Students also attempted significantly more questions than those in the GenAI tutor condition in Section 1 and the Internet condition in Section 2. Post-task responses also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses and the highest proportion of calm responses in the Human condition, adding an affective dimension to this more favourable profile. While these patterns do not establish greater conceptual progress because response accuracy and learning were not assessed, they may reflect more extensive scaffolding and co-regulatory support under human tutoring. Within this broader pattern, lower effort in the Human condition may indicate that less exertion was required to continue when support made the tasks feel more manageable, rather than reduced engagement. Viewed through this theoretical lens, the pattern observed in the GenAI tutor condition is consistent with accounts of a distinct and partial form of emerging co-regulation, rather than the fuller scaffolding and co-regulatory capacities associated with human tutoring. In contrast, the pattern under human tutoring was more consistent with scaffolding and coregulation operating together. Comparable dissociations have been observed in recent experimental studies of AI-supported learning, where improvements in affective experience under AI support were not accompanied by gains in conceptual understanding (Bassner et al., 2026) , and where AI support was associated with motivational and affective benefits while lacking the social presence and collaborative depth of human interaction (Fan et al., 2025) . Together, these patterns are consistent with positioning generative AI between human support and independent internet search along a continuum of scaffolding and coregulation. Because conceptual progress and learning were not assessed, this positioning concerns engagement with difficulty rather than comparative learning effectiveness. Figure 1 provides a schematic summary of this interpretive positioning. By comparing human tutoring, the GenAI tutor used in this study and internet-based support under controlled conditions, this study contributes empirical evidence relevant to socio-cognitive accounts of challenge and to the idea
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be noted. The study was a single-session experiment conducted in one high-attaining, digitally confident sixth-form college. Participation was self-selecting and large proportions of the sample studied Mathematics and science subjects. Although Mathematics and Further Mathematics participation did not differ significantly across conditions, this subject profile may limit the generalisability of the findings to students with different academic backgrounds. The findings may also not generalise to contexts in which baseline self-regulation or digital familiarity is lower or to longer-term classroom settings. Effort, perceived difficulty and stress were measured using single-item self-reports, with stress assessed only once, and tasks were intentionally set above curriculum level, which may have amplified challenge-related responses. Regulatory processes were inferred indirectly through behavioural and affective indicators rather than measured directly. The number of questions attempted did not capture the accuracy or quality of students' responses. A higher number of attempts could therefore reflect productive persistence, superficial movement between questions or unproductive floundering. Attempts should consequently be interpreted as a behavioural indicator of engagement across the task, rather than as evidence of successful task progress, conceptual understanding or learning. Interaction logs and transcripts were not included in the analysis, and the frequency, content and quality of support interactions were therefore not compared systematically across conditions. Consequently, scaffolding, co-regulation and learning partnership are used as theoretical lenses for interpreting the observed patterns, rather than as processes demonstrated by the study. Support-specific factors also warrant consideration. As support was provided by a single tutor, his individual style and physical presence may have shaped participants' interactions and responses to challenge. His presence may have offered reassurance or encouraged persistence, while obtaining help required direct social interaction. By contrast, students could consult the GenAI tutor without initiating a direct social interaction whenever they wished. Responses to the GenAI tutor may also have been influenced by novelty (Fryer et al., 2017) , while the Internet condition reflected the variable quality of open web resources. Finally, because the precise underlying model snapshot and behavioural configuration were not available to the researchers, and changes during the data-collection period could not be ruled out, the findings concern Khanmigo Lite as accessed between November 2024 and July 2025. They should not be generalised uncritically to other versions of Khanmigo Lite or to GenAI tutors as a category. Differences between these conditions may therefore reflect both the source of support and how that support was accessed. Despite these limitations, the findings have implications for how challenge is supported and experienced in educational contexts. For teachers, the results suggest that support should be treated as a pedagogical decision that shapes learners' engagement with difficulty, not simply as a means of providing answers. This points to a complementary role for AI tutors alongside human instruction, where AI may support learners in continuing to invest effort during challenging independent work, while teachers monitor whether difficulty is being resolved and provide responsive support when needed. For learners, the study highlights that responses to difficulty are not solely individual traits but are shaped by the support context, underscoring the importance of developing awareness of how different forms of help influence effort, persistence and stress. This suggests value in explicitly teaching helpseeking strategies, including how to engage productively with AI tutors as a way of working through difficulty rather than bypassing challenge. More broadly, the results underscore the value of attending to learners' behavioural and affective responses when evaluating the educational impact of AI.

summary.idea: Hard math felt more difficult with an AI tutor than with a human tutor on the second set of problems.
summary.explain: Students worked through two sets of unfamiliar math problems. The experiment asked how they responded when the work got hard and which difficulty levels they chose afterward.
summary.approach: Researchers randomly assigned students aged 16–18 at one English sixth-form college to a human math tutor, Khanmigo Lite or independent internet search. The main analysis included 149 students. Each set lasted 20 minutes.

items.title: Teacher-regulated generative AI in structured group tasks: independent performance and metacognitive judgements in higher education
items.abstract_text: Introduction As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education classrooms, an important question is whether it shapes not only students' task performance but also how they judge their own learning. This study examined whether participation in AI-supported structured group tasks was associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. Methods A group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design was implemented in two undergraduate classes using Rain Classroom, a digital instructional platform. Students worked in pre-existing groups, and instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level. In the AI-supported condition, students were permitted to use the platform's built-in AI learning companion during structured group discussion; in the non-AI-supported condition, they were instructed not to use it. After previewing the post-task assessment items, students completed a task-specific judgement form before responding to the assessment itself. The final analytic sample consisted of 126 students. Results Linear mixed models accounting for class and group-level clustering indicated significantly higher independent post-task performance in the AI-supported condition, B = 0.506, SE = 0.188, p = 0.013, 95% CI [0.117, 0.894], with a small descriptive standardized mean difference ( d = 0.196). No statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence judgements, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Discussion These findings indicate a modest between-condition difference in post-task performance without parallel statistically detectable differences in metacognitive monitoring.

Students worked in pre-existing groups, and instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level. In the AI-supported condition, students were permitted to use the platform's built-in AI learning companion during structured group discussion; in the non-AI-supported condition, they were instructed not to use it. After previewing the post-task assessment items, students completed a task-specific judgement form before responding to the assessment itself. The final analytic sample consisted of 126 students. Results: Linear mixed models accounting for class and group-level clustering indicated significantly higher independent post-task performance in the AIsupported condition, B = 0.506, SE = 0.188, p = 0.013, 95% CI [0.117, 0.894], with a small descriptive standardized mean difference (d = 0.196). No statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence judgements, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Discussion: These findings indicate a modest between-condition difference in post-task performance without parallel statistically detectable differences in metacognitive monitoring. This study adopted a group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design to examine whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration compared with non-AI-supported structured group tasks. The study was conducted in two undergraduate classes within the same university course. Students completed the same instructional task under one of two conditions: an AI-supported condition or a non-AI-supported condition. Because the intervention was implemented through group-based classroom activity, instructional condition was randomly assigned at the group level, whereas the main outcome variables were measured at the individual level through a task-specific judgement form and an individual post-task assessment. The design was intended to preserve ecological validity while maintaining reasonable control over the role of AI in classroom learning by embedding AI as a regulated support resource during structured group discussion rather than as an unrestricted answergenerating tool. Because no pre-intervention measures of the study outcomes were collected, the design does not permit direct assessment of baseline equivalence or within-student change over time. Participants were undergraduate students enrolled in a university course taught by the researcher. During the semester, the researcher taught five sections of the course, from which two intact classes were randomly selected for inclusion in the study. The study was conducted in March 2026 in regular classroom settings and was embedded within normal teaching activities. All participants were second-year undergraduates majoring in Business English or Secretarial Studies. Age and gender were not collected as study variables. At the beginning of the semester, students in each class had already formed their own discussion groups for routine classroom activities. Group formation was based on students' free choice, and some students chose to work individually; as a result, group size ranged from 1 to 8 students. Of the 28 pre-existing groups, three were single-person groups: one was assigned to the AIsupported condition and two to the non-AI-supported condition. The remaining 25 groups consisted of two to eight students. These naturally formed groups were retained for the present study in order to preserve the ecological validity of the instructional context and to respect students' original grouping preferences. At the time of randomization, each class consisted of 14 pre-existing groups, resulting in 28 groups across the two classes. The first class included 86 enrolled students, whereas the second class included 67 students. Of these, 139 students initially consented to participate. Participation was entirely voluntary, and students were informed that choosing not to participate would not affect their course grades or academic evaluation in any way. The flow of participants from initial enrolment to the final analytic sample is shown in Figure 1 . Because the instructional intervention was implemented during small-group discussion, the pre-existing discussion groups, rather than individual students, served as the units of randomization. The 28 groups from the two classes were pooled and allocated to the two instructional conditions in SPSS using an overall 1:1 restricted randomization procedure. Class was not used as a stratification factor. This resulted in 14 groups being assigned to the AIsupported condition and 14 to the non-AI-supported condition. In Class 1, five groups were allocated to the AI-supported condition and nine to the non-AI-supported condition; in Class 2, nine groups were allocated to the AI-supported condition and five to the non-AI-supported condition. Because the pre-existing groups varied in size, group-level randomization did not produce equal numbers of individual students across the class-by-condition cells. After exclusions due to withdrawal or incomplete data, the final analytic sample consisted of 126 students, including 62 in the AI-supported condition and 64 in the non-AI-supported Flow of participants through the study. condition (see Figure 1 ). Detailed exclusion reasons and their distribution by class and instructional condition are reported in Supplementary Appendix K. Missing outcome data were not imputed, and the primary analyses were conducted using complete cases. These exclusions left 27 analytic groups (13 AI-supported and 14 non-AI-supported), as one AI-supported group in Class 2 had no remaining analysable participants. The overall exclusion proportions did not differ significantly by instructional condition, χ 2 (1, N = 139) = 0.717, p = 0.397; however, this comparison does not rule out the possibility of attrition-related bias. No exclusions were made on the basis of detected use of the Rain Classroom AI learning companion outside the assigned condition, as no such platform-based violations were identified in the usage records. The instructional activity was implemented through Rain Classroom, a smart teaching platform commonly used in Chinese higher education (Li et al., 2022; Lv et al., 2024) . The platform was used to deliver the case materials, organize the structured group discussion, administer the judgement form, and collect students' responses to the individual post-task assessment. The study was embedded in a course session focusing on life and wellbeing, and the instructional task was designed to align with this instructional theme while remaining standardized across the two classes. The study was conducted during regular 90-min class sessions and followed a standardized procedure across both classes. The five core study stages accounted for 80 min. The remaining approximately 10 min were used for routine procedural instructions and transitions between activities, including access to Rain Classroom and movement between the discussion, judgement, and assessment stages. analysis.results: In contrast to the significant difference in independent posttask performance, the adjusted between-condition difference in predicted score was not statistically significant. Neither confidence in anticipated performance nor confidence in understanding differed significantly between conditions. Thus, although the AIsupported group obtained higher actual post-task scores, the present data provide no statistically detectable evidence that AIsupported discussion also changed students' prospective estimates of performance or their immediate subjective certainty about performance and understanding. One explanation is that performance predictions and confidence judgements are shaped by more than informational support alone (Lichtenstein and Fischhoff, 1977) . In classroom settings, such judgements may reflect habitual self-evaluative tendencies, perceived task difficulty, prior academic experience, and personal standards for determining whether sufficient understanding has been achieved (Nederhand et al., 2021) . A single episode of AI-supported discussion may therefore support task preparation without being sufficient to produce a clearly detectable shift in students' prospective self-evaluations. The timing of the judgement form may also be relevant. Students completed it after viewing the assessment items but before answering them, a procedure designed to capture taskspecific judgements rather than general attitudes toward AI. Their predictions and confidence ratings may therefore have reflected a relatively cautious appraisal of the specific assessment they were about to complete rather than a broader sense of ease or familiarity associated with AI support. In this sense, the measures captured a more immediate task-specific judgement than broader self-report measures commonly used in studies of AI adoption or attitudes (Double, 2025; Schraw, 2009) . From a distributed cognition perspective, it is plausible that access to shared cognitive resources supported task preparation without necessarily changing students' personal estimates of their own performance. Because the study did not measure how individual students appropriated peer or AI contributions, this remains an interpretive possibility rather than a tested mechanism (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Atchley et al., 2024; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022 Kim et al., , 2025)) . Taken together, these findings show that higher observed performance in the AI-supported condition was not accompanied by statistically detectable differences in predicted performance or confidence. The confidence intervals around the prediction and confidence estimates all included zero and remained sufficiently wide to indicate uncertainty about the magnitude of any betweencondition differences. Given the limited number of analytic groups and the absence of an a priori power calculation, these non-significant findings should not be interpreted as evidence that the conditions were equivalent; rather, the present study did not detect parallel changes in students' immediate prospective judgements. The study also found no statistically significant differences between the AI-supported and non-AI-supported conditions in either calibration bias or absolute calibration error. The corresponding descriptive effect sizes were small (d = 0.227 for calibration bias; d = -0.144 for absolute calibration error). Thus, although students in the AI-supported condition performed significantly better on the post-task assessment, they did not show statistically detectable greater accuracy in judging their own performance than students in the non-AI-supported condition. This pattern is consistent with the distinction between task performance and metacognitive accuracy (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Schraw, 2009) . AI-supported discussion may assist task preparation without necessarily changing the processes students use to evaluate how well they are likely to perform. Performance and accurate self-monitoring should therefore not be assumed to develop in parallel. One explanation is that cognitive calibration requires more than informational assistance or discussion support (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024) . Better calibration may require explicit opportunities to compare judgements with outcomes, reflect on the basis of confidence, and evaluate the limits of one's understanding (Wang et al., 2024) . In the present study, the Rain Classroom AI learning companion supported group discussion but was not designed specifically to prompt metacognitive reflection, confidence checking, or prediction-feedback comparison. The instructional design therefore targeted task engagement more directly than calibration processes. Distributed cognition provides a contextual rather than causal interpretation of this result. The AI-supported task made information and interpretive resources available across peers, task materials, and the AI tool (Aarset and Johannessen, 2022; Hollan et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2022) , but the study did not directly assess whether or how these shared resources were internalized by individual students. It is therefore possible that collaborative resources supported task processing without producing a corresponding difference in individual metacognitive monitoring, but this mechanism remains to be tested directly (Atchley et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2024) . The short-term nature of the activity may also be relevant. Calibration depends on the alignment between subjective judgement and actual performance and may require repeated cycles of prediction, action, feedback, and revision before measurable change becomes visible (Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Wang et al., 2024) . A single classroom session may therefore be more likely to reveal an immediate performance difference than a stable change in monitoring accuracy. Because both predicted and actual performance were measured on bounded 0-10 scales, and actual scores showed substantial upper-end concentration, the derived calibration indices also had constrained score distributions, which may have reduced their sensitivity to between-condition differences. The non-significant calibration findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously. They provide no evidence that the present form of AI-supported discussion improved calibration accuracy, while the brief intervention and restricted score variability may have limited sensitivity to detect such differences. If improved judgement accuracy is an instructional goal, additional metacognitive scaffolding may be needed alongside AI-supported task activities. Taken together, this differentiated pattern suggests a theoretically important distinction between externally supported task processing and internally calibrated self-monitoring. In a structured collaborative task, AI may expand the informational and interpretive resources available to the group, but the present findings do not establish whether such support changes individual metacognitive monitoring.
analysis.discussion: This study examined whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration. The findings revealed a differentiated pattern across outcomes. Students in the AI-supported condition obtained significantly higher scores on the independent post-task assessment than those in the non-AIsupported condition. However, no statistically significant betweencondition differences were found in predicted score, confidence in anticipated performance, confidence in understanding, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. Taken together, the statistically detectable difference was concentrated at the level of independent task performance rather than extending to students' prospective judgements or metacognitive accuracy. This pattern underscores the importance of examining performance and metacognitive monitoring as related but distinct outcomes of AI-supported classroom activity. This study examined whether AI-supported structured group tasks were associated with differences in university students' independent post-task performance, performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration in a higher education classroom. Using a group-randomized, post-test-only classroom design implemented through Rain Classroom, the analysis indicated that students in the AI-supported condition obtained higher scores on the independent post-task assessment than those in the non-AI-supported condition. However, no statistically significant between-condition differences were observed in predicted performance, confidence in anticipated performance, confidence in understanding, calibration bias, or absolute calibration error. These findings indicate that, in the present instructional context, the AI-supported condition was associated with modestly higher performance on this task-specific assessment, without statistically detectable between-condition differences in performance predictions, confidence judgements, or cognitive calibration. Overall, the findings highlight the value of distinguishing task performance from metacognitive monitoring as separate outcomes when evaluating AI-supported classroom activities in higher education.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations of the present study should be considered when interpreting the findings, with the most consequential relating to study design, measurement, and statistical precision. First, no pre-intervention measures of content knowledge, confidence, or calibration were collected. Consequently, although random assignment occurred at the group level, it cannot be determined with certainty whether the two instructional conditions were fully equivalent on these variables prior to the intervention. This limits the strength of causal inference that can be drawn from the observed post-task differences. Future research could incorporate pre-and post-intervention measures in order to examine more directly how AI-supported structured group tasks influence change over time in both learning outcomes and metacognitive judgements. Second, the post-task assessment was intentionally brief and designed for classroom implementation. Although this format suited the practical constraints of a single class session and aligned closely with the instructional task, it should be interpreted as a task-specific indicator of learning rather than as a fully validated standardized measure. Because the assessment consisted of only four heterogeneous items, score precision may have been limited, and individual items may have had a relatively strong influence on total scores. Because item-level scores were not retained in the analytic dataset, item-specific performance patterns could not be examined retrospectively. The score distribution also showed notable upper-end concentration: 27.8% of the full sample obtained the maximum score, and ceiling concentration was particularly pronounced in the Class 1 AI-supported subgroup, where 69.0% obtained the maximum. This restricted variability may have reduced sensitivity for estimating between-condition differences in performance and, because calibration indices were derived from predicted and actual scores on the same bounded 0-10 scale, may also have constrained calibration-related outcomes. Although inter-rater reliability for the application/transfer item was excellent for the mean of the two ratings, ICC (A,2) = 0.935, 95% CI [0.890, 0.955], the brevity, heterogeneity, and upper-end concentration of the assessment remain important constraints. Future research could employ more extensive outcome measures with greater discrimination at the upper end. Third, no a priori power analysis was conducted. Together with the limited number of analytic groups, this means that the study may have had limited statistical precision for detecting small or moderate between-condition differences in performance predictions, confidence, or calibration. The non-significant findings should accordingly be interpreted as an absence of statistically detectable differences in this sample rather than as evidence of equivalence between conditions. Future studies should use larger samples, prospectively justified sample sizes, and repeated assessments to provide a more precise account of how AI-supported learning relates to both performance and metacognitive monitoring. Fourth, the study was conducted by the researcher acting as the course instructor. Although this arrangement supported implementation within an authentic teaching context, it also introduced the possibility of instructor-related bias. The dual role of researcher and instructor may have influenced instructional delivery, participant expectations, or intervention fidelity in subtle but unmeasured ways. Future research could reduce this source of bias by involving independent instructors, using multiple instructors, or adopting designs in which implementation and analysis are more clearly separated. Fifth, although the study examined performance predictions, confidence judgements, and cognitive calibration in addition to performance, it did not capture fine-grained interaction data on how groups actually used the AI support during discussion. For example, the study did not analyse the specific prompts students entered, the types of responses generated by the AI learning companion, or the extent to which different groups relied on AI in different ways. As a result, the present findings can describe between-condition differences, but cannot identify the detailed mechanisms through which those differences emerged. Future research could incorporate process-oriented data such as prompt logs, interaction traces, discussion transcripts, or response uptake patterns to move beyond whether conditions differ and toward a more precise understanding of how different forms of human-AI interaction relate to performance and metacognitive outcomes. Sixth, the AI support examined in this study was the Rain Classroom AI learning companion, embedded within a specific classroom platform and used under teacher-regulated conditions. The comparison in this study was therefore based on permitted vs. non-permitted use of a platform-embedded AI tool within a structured classroom task, rather than on unrestricted use of external generative AI systems. In addition, the intervention was relatively short in duration, as the study focused on a single classroom-based activity. As a result, the findings should not be taken as applying equally to all forms of generative AI or to more open-ended, sustained, or student-directed AI use. Future research could compare different AI systems, interaction conditions, and intervention durations in order to clarify how different AI affordances and instructional arrangements shape both learning outcomes and metacognitive processes (Atchley et al., 2024; Bauer et al., 2025; Janssen and Lazonder, 2024; Kim et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024) . Seventh, the study was conducted in a specific instructional context, namely a university course session on life and wellbeing, using a single case-based structured group task. Although this context provided an authentic classroom setting for examining AI-supported learning, the findings should not be assumed to generalize directly to other subjects, task types, or higher education contexts. The role of AI support may differ across disciplines, especially in courses characterized by different epistemic demands, problem-solving requirements, or assessment forms (Bond et al., 2024; Qian, 2025) . Future research could therefore examine whether the present pattern of findings is specific to this course theme and task design or reflects a more general feature of AIsupported structured group learning across disciplinary contexts.

items.title: Editorial: Harnessing AI to support self-regulated learning in educational and workplace settings

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The Research Topic begins with Achuthan's Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning, which provides a broad empirical examination of the relationship between AI and learner autonomy. Synthesizing 32 empirical studies, 92 effect sizes, and 3,029 participants, the study examines the effects of AI-based interventions on SRL, self-directed learning (SDL), different dimensions and phases of SRL, and learning outcomes. The findings indicate positive effects of AI interventions on overall SRL and SDL, with particularly notable effects during the forethought phase, including goal setting and planning. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. The findings therefore provide encouraging evidence for AI as a scaffold for self-regulation while highlighting the importance of designing support across the full SRL cycle.Building on this macro-level evidence, Agustin's AI as a co-regulator: relational design for strengthening self-regulated learning addresses the theoretical mechanics of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices, stigma, and selfregulated learning in higher education examines the affective, social, and institutional factors that influence how learners adopt these tools in practice. Focusing on undergraduate students at a Canadian university, the authors explore the intersection of student AI disclosure practices, social stigma, and SRL processes. Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Highly anxious students who use AI heavily are more likely to conceal their usage or restrict sharing to peer networks. This study highlights that technical scaffolds cannot succeed in a vacuum; institutional policies and pedagogical environments must account for emotional and social dynamics to prevent secrecy from undermining reflective SRL practices.Considered together, the four articles in this Research Topic illustrate that AI's role in self-regulated learning extends far beyond simple automation or content delivery. Achuthan's meta-analysis provides evidence of AI's potential to strengthen SRL and SDL, while also identifying limitations in behavioral regulation. Agustin's framework addresses this challenge conceptually by positioning AI as a co-regulator that supports learners without displacing their agency. Gu et al. demonstrate how such support can be enacted in feedback processes, whereas Chang et al. show how emotions, stigma, and institutional expectations shape learners' decisions about AI use. This collection highlights that realizing the promise of AI-supported self-regulated learning requires more than personalization or automation. Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static …
items.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

reading.methods: Spatial ability is a well-established predictor of performance in multimedia learning, particularly for materials involving threedimensional structures, mental rotation, and assembly processes (Uttal et al., 2013; Voyer et al., 1995) . Although average gender differences in spatial ability have been reported, they are small to moderate, highly variable across tasks and contexts, and often confounded with prior experience, technology familiarity, and confidence (Bartlett and Camba, 2023; Castro-Alonso et al., 2019) . Therefore, gender should be treated as an observed grouping variable rather than a causal or biological determinant. Research on gender and educational technology also suggests that male and female learners may differ in technology acceptance, visual search habits, and preferences for dynamic versus static representations, but these differences are context-dependent and should not be used to prescribe different treatments based solely on gender (Wang H. et al., 2023; Wang J. et al., 2023; Qazi et al., 2022; Tandrayen-Ragoobur and Gokulsing, 2022) . For inclusive educational design, the goal is not to design "for males" or "for females," but to identify when motion helps or hinders different learners and to provide learner-controlled or adaptive options (Castro-Alonso et al., 2021) . This perspective motivates the present examination of whether responses to motion-enhanced AI-generated images differ across observed gender groups. This study employed a 2 × 2 between
reading.findings: A 2 (gender group: male vs. female) × 2 (presentation condition: static vs. motion-enhanced) between-subjects design was implemented. Data were analyzed using two-way ANOVA in SPSS 27 software. Significant effects were further examined via simpleeffects tests and simple main effect analyses to delineate differences between factor levels. The analysis estimated main and interaction effects of gender differences and motion-enhanced AI-generated images on participants' learning performance (accuracy rate) and learning experience. The significance level was set at α = 0.05. The significant effect was further analyzed with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons (These contrasts include 95% confidence intervals) to help address the differences among the factor levels. Because multiple subjective outcomes were examined, these analyses were treated as exploratory. No omnibus multiplicity correction was applied across all dependent variables; therefore, nominal p-values for secondary outcomes should be interpreted cautiously. Bonferroni adjustment was applied to simple-effect comparisons following significant interactions.
reading.interpretation: Before discussing the implications of our findings, it is important to define the scope within which these results are most directly applicable. This study examined a specific type of instructional contentvisuospatially complex material (mortise and tenon structures) requiring understanding of three-dimensional relationships and assembly processes. The participants were higher education students with no prior domain knowledge, and the instructional videos were brief (140 s) and delivered on mobile devices. Therefore, our findings are most directly relevant to similar learning contexts: technical or procedural knowledge domains, novice learners, and short-format mobile learning environments. The present study investigated the effects of motion-enhanced AI-generated images in instructional videos on learning performance and subjective experience, with a particular focus on genderbased differences. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), this research aimed to elucidate whether dynamic visual presentations differentially impact male and female learners. The findings reveal a nuanced pattern: while motion effects alone did not significantly enhance learning accuracy, gender was associated with differences in objective performance and subjective evaluations. Significant interaction effects between gender and motion effects were observed for acceptability and mental effort, suggesting that responses to dynamic visual information may differ across gender groups; however, these differences should be interpreted cautiously because gender was not experimentally manipulated and relevant covariates were not measured. reading.limitations: Several limitations qualify the findings of this study and should be considered when interpreting the results. First, no formal manipulation check or independent image-quality assessment was conducted. We did not collect expert or participant ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, or informational equivalence between the static and dynamic conditions. Although images were informally screened for visible artifacts and structural accuracy before inclusion, this screening served only as a material-selection step and does not constitute formal validation. We therefore cannot conclusively verify that participants perceived the static/dynamic distinction as intended, nor can we fully rule out artifact-related confounding. Future research should include manipulation checks and systematic ratings of visual quality, structural accuracy, semantic consistency, motion salience, and informational equivalence. analysis.methods: Spatial ability is a well-established predictor of performance in multimedia learning, particularly for materials involving threedimensional structures, mental rotation, and assembly processes (Uttal et al., 2013; Voyer et al., 1995) . Although average gender differences in spatial ability have been reported, they are small to moderate, highly variable across tasks and contexts, and often confounded with prior experience, technology familiarity, and confidence (Bartlett and Camba, 2023; Castro-Alonso et al., 2019) . Therefore, gender should be treated as an observed grouping variable rather than a causal or biological determinant. Research on gender and educational technology also suggests that male and female learners may differ in technology acceptance, visual search habits, and preferences for dynamic versus static representations, but these differences are context-dependent and should not be used to prescribe different treatments based solely on gender (Wang H. et al., 2023; Wang J. et al., 2023; Qazi et al., 2022; Tandrayen-Ragoobur and Gokulsing, 2022) . For inclusive educational design, the goal is not to design "for males" or "for females," but to identify when motion helps or hinders different learners and to provide learner-controlled or adaptive options (Castro-Alonso et al., 2021) . This perspective motivates the present examination of whether responses to motion-enhanced AI-generated images differ across observed gender groups. This study employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design, with two independent variables: "motion-enhanced AI-generated images" (static/dynamic) and "gender differences" (male/female). During the experimental design process, Illustrator software was used for graphic design, and CapCut was employed to produce the instructional videos. The experiment was conducted on an iPhone 11 device running iOS 15.7, featuring a 6.1 -inch Liquid Retina HD display. Participants watched an instructional video and subsequently completed a 10-item true/false test and a psychological evaluation questionnaire (collecting subjective data). Specifically, the dependent variables were learning accuracy, willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and perceived mental effort. Figure 1 shows the research framework of this study. Using purposive sampling, 40 undergraduate students (20 male; 20 female) were recruited via advertisement from a university in Shenzhen, China. A 2 (Gender: Male/Female) × 2 (Condition: Static/ Dynamic) between-subjects design was used. Forty participants were evenly distributed across the four experimental cells (Static-Male/ Static-Female/Dynamic-Male/Dynamic-Female), with n = 10 per cell. Stratified randomization was employed: participants were first stratified by gender, then randomly assigned to the static or dynamic video condition within each stratum. To control for prior knowledge, participants were explicitly screened to ensure they had no background in furniture design, woodworking, or architectural engineering, and specifically no prior knowledge of "mortise and tenon" structures. All participants possessed normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Before the experiment began, the researcher thoroughly explained the experimental purpose and safeguards. After fully understanding the relevant information, participants voluntarily signed a written informed consent form, confirming their rights to voluntary participation, informed consent, and withdrawal. Additionally, to avoid practice effects on the experimental results, all participants were first-time viewers of the experimental videos and were native Chinese speakers. All experimental protocols were approved by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Technology University under Approval No. SZTUYXLL2025113, a named institutional committee. Furthermore, written informed consent was obtained from all participants before participation. The experimental materials consisted of two versions of an online instructional video course on mortise-tenon structures. The visual assets were generated using a two-step workflow involving AI generation and manual editing to ensure both technical quality and pedagogical relevance. To ensure reproducibility and transparency, the AI-generated visual assets were created using Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) through the Automatic1111 web interface. A structured prompting strategy was employed to ensure high fidelity and structural accuracy. Positive prompts emphasized exploded views of mortise-tenon joints, traditional Chinese woodworking, an isometric perspective, and 8 k resolution on a white background. Negative prompts excluded distorted structures, artifacts, text, and cartoonish styles. The generation parameters were as follows: Euler a sampler, 50 sampling steps, CFG scale of 7.5, and a resolution of 1,024 × 1,024 pixels. A total of 50 image generations were produced per visual scene to allow for a rigorous selection process. The selection criterion was based on a "qualityfirst" approach: generated images were first filtered for visual fidelity, Before the commencement of the experiment, participants were thoroughly briefed on its purpose and other pertinent details. Specifically, they first completed an informed consent form and a background information questionnaire. Subsequently, they watched a 140-s instructional video on mortise-tenon structures in full-screen mode, viewing it only once. The video systematically showcased various mortise-tenon jointing methods, arranged in ascending order of difficulty, and was accompanied by detailed textual explanations elucidating their features, principles, and applications. Following the video, participants undertook three assessment sections: (1) Learning Effectiveness Test: The two prototypes used in this experiment. This section comprised 10 true/false questions, each worth 1 point (totaling 10 points), designed to evaluate participants' knowledge of mortise-tenon structure types, principles, and applications. This assessment method has a robust application history in similar research (Chen et al., 2025) . To ensure content validity, the video script and questions underwent review by three senior experts in furniture design instruction, each boasting over 15 years of experience, to confirm alignment with the learning objectives.
